title: DeepSeek-V4-Pro Ships for Real: 1.7T Under MIT
hook: The preview is over. DeepSeek's 1.7-trillion-parameter MoE lands with open MIT weights, built-in speculative decoding, and benchmark claims aimed straight at the closed frontier.
key_points: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 supersedes the preview release, with the model card citing improved agentic capability.
1.7 trillion parameters in a mixture-of-experts design; deployment guidance covers expert parallelism across vLLM and SGLang.
Ships a DSpark speculative decoding module as part of the model rather than as a separate serving trick.
Three reasoning effort levels (low, high, max), with a recommended maximum output length of 384K tokens at high and max.
Reported benchmarks: HLE with tools 60.0, Terminal Bench 2.1 87.9, NL2Repo 61.5, DeepSWE 62.7.
Released under the MIT license — unusually permissive for a model at this scale.
content_html: DeepSeek's V4-Pro moved from preview to a dated release, DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, with weights on Hugging Face under the MIT license. The model card describes a 1.7-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts with improved agentic capability over the preview, three selectable reasoning effort levels, and a bundled DSpark speculative decoding module — fast decoding shipped as part of the model instead of left to whoever serves it.
extra_html:
DeepSeek's own reported numbers are agent- and code-heavy: 60.0 on HLE with tools, 87.9 on Terminal Bench 2.1, 61.5 on NL2Repo, and 62.7 on DeepSWE. The card claims the release outperforms the preview and is "broadly competitive with the strongest proprietary models available"; those are vendor claims on vendor-selected benchmarks, so the usual caution applies until independent evaluations land.

The practical shape of this release: deployment guidance targets vLLM and SGLang with expert parallelism, and a recommended output ceiling of 384K tokens at high and max reasoning effort. A 1.7T MoE is not a laptop model regardless of sparsity, but MIT terms at frontier scale mean the barrier is GPUs rather than permission.

related.title: DeepSeek-V4: Sparse Attention, Million-Token Default
related.hook: DeepSeek-V4 makes a 1M-token context window the default and pairs token-wise compression with sparse attention, so long-context inference no longer pays the usual compute and memory tax.

related.title: DSpark: The Speculative Decoder Behind DeepSeek's Production Serving
related.hook: Parallel drafters draft fast, but verifying all of it wastes capacity on likely rejects. DSpark schedules verification by confidence — and cut DeepSeek-V4's per-user latency 60-85% in production.

related.title: What Is a Mixture of Experts?
related.hook: Instead of running every input through one big network, route each token to a few specialist sub-networks - total capacity grows without proportional compute.

flashcards.prompt: What is unusual about how DeepSeek-V4-Pro handles speculative decoding?

choices.text: A DSpark speculative decoding module ships as part of the model itself
It rejects speculative decoding as incompatible with mixture-of-experts routing
It requires a separately trained draft model from a third party

flashcards.explanation_html: Speculative decoding is usually a serving-layer choice bolted on afterward. Bundling DSpark into the release makes fast decoding part of the model's contract rather than the deployer's problem.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the MIT license matter for a 1.7T-parameter model?
flashcards.back_html: At this scale most releases carry custom or restricted terms. MIT means no usage restrictions on a model competitive with closed frontier systems — the constraint on using it becomes hardware, not legal.

flashcards.prompt: What do the three reasoning effort levels imply about serving this model?
flashcards.back_html: Compute per query is a deployment dial, not a fixed property: low, high, and max trade latency and token spend against answer quality, with output length recommendations up to 384K tokens at the higher settings.
